title: Deductions from Gross Total Income
outcomes: Apply the general principles of Chapter VIII.
Compute deductions for payments and investments.
Apply health, disability and interest deductions.
Apply deductions for start-ups, employment and other incomes.

meta.exam_tip: Confirm the regime first; most personal deductions vanish under section 202(1).

concepts.title: General principles of Chapter VIII deductions
body: Chapter VIII deductions are made from gross total income; their total cannot exceed GTI, and they are not allowed against special-rate incomes such as STCG under section 196, LTCG under sections 197 and 198, or casual winnings.

Most deductions (sections 123, 124(3), 126–135, 153, 154) are unavailable under the default regime of section 202(1). Employer NPS contribution under section 124(1) and additional employee cost under section 146 remain available under it.

For profit-linked deductions in Part C, the return must be filed by the due date under section 263(1), the same profits cannot be claimed twice, and audit reports must be furnished where required (section 122).
concepts.analogy: Deductions come off GTI, never off special-rate income.
concepts.work: A salaried person in the default regime can still claim the employer's NPS contribution.

concepts.title: Deductions for payments and investments
body: Section 123: payments such as life insurance premiums (within premium-to-sum assured limits), PPF, EPF, ELSS, NSC, tuition fees, housing loan principal and Sukanya Samriddhi deposits qualify, up to ₹1,50,000 for individuals and HUFs.

Section 124: employer contribution to NPS up to 14% of salary for government employers and 10% for others (14% for employees under the default regime); the employee's own contribution qualifies within ₹1,50,000 and an extra ₹50,000 under section 124(3).
Section 129 allows interest on education loans for higher studies for up to 8 years; sections 130 to 132 deal with specified housing loans and electric vehicle loan interest as provided.
concepts.analogy: Saving-linked deductions mainly sit in sections 123 and 124.
concepts.work: PPF of ₹1 lakh plus LIC premium of ₹80,000 yields a deduction of ₹1.5 lakh.

concepts.title: Health, disability and other personal deductions
body: Section 126 (health insurance): up to ₹25,000 for self, spouse and dependent children (₹50,000 if any is a senior citizen), and another ₹25,000/₹50,000 for parents; preventive health check-up within these limits; payment other than in cash, except for check-ups.

Section 127 (maintenance or medical treatment of a dependant with disability): flat ₹75,000, or ₹1,25,000 for severe disability. Section 154 (assessee himself with disability): the same amounts. Section 128 (specified diseases): actual expenditure up to ₹40,000, or ₹1,00,000 for senior citizens, net of insurance reimbursements.
Section 153: interest on savings accounts up to ₹10,000 for individuals (non-senior) and HUFs; up to ₹50,000 on all deposits for resident senior citizens.
concepts.analogy: Health and disability deductions have fixed caps.
concepts.work: Parents' policy of ₹55,000 for seniors gives ₹50,000.

concepts.title: Donations and rent
body: Section 133 (donations): donations to specified funds and institutions qualify at 100% or 50%, with or without a ceiling of 10% of adjusted gross total income depending on the category; cash donations above ₹2,000 are not allowed; unavailable to individuals, HUFs and similar persons in the default regime and to companies on concessional regimes.

Section 134 (rent paid): for those not receiving HRA and not owning a residence at the place of work, the deduction is the least of rent minus 10% of total income, 25% of total income and ₹5,000 a month, with a declaration in the prescribed form.

Sections 135 to 137: donations for scientific research or rural development (for those without business income) and contributions to political parties or electoral trusts (other than in cash) are deductible.
concepts.analogy: Donations by banking modes; rent relief has a three-way cap.
concepts.work: Rent of ₹15,000 a month with total income of ₹6 lakh gives a deduction of ₹60,000.

concepts.title: Deductions in respect of certain incomes
body: Section 140: an eligible start-up (company or LLP incorporated between 1 April 2016 and 31 March 2030, turnover up to ₹300 crore, with a certificate from the Inter-Ministerial Board) can deduct 100% of profits for any 3 consecutive years out of the first 10.

Section 146: assessees subject to tax audit can deduct 30% of additional employee cost for 3 years from the year of employment, if the business is not formed by splitting or reconstruction and a CA report is furnished. Section 148 deducts inter-corporate dividends redistributed within the specified time.

Other income-based deductions include co-operative society income (section 149), royalty on books and patents (sections 151 and 152), and specified IFSC units, SEZ and infrastructure undertakings (sections 138, 139, 144, 147) as provided.
concepts.analogy: Profit-linked deductions reward start-ups, jobs and specific sectors.
concepts.work: Additional employee cost of ₹40 lakh gives ₹12 lakh a year for three years.

illustrations.title: Personal deductions under the optional regime
illustrations.q: Harish, 45, has opted out of the default regime for T.Y. 2026-27. He pays: PPF ₹1,00,000; life insurance premium ₹80,000 (within the premium limits); own NPS ₹50,000 (not claimed elsewhere); health insurance for self and family ₹30,000; health insurance for his parents (both above 60) ₹55,000; and has savings bank interest of ₹14,000. Compute total Chapter VIII deductions.

illustrations.title: Rent paid without HRA
illustrations.q: Ishita, a self-employed designer under the optional regime, pays rent of ₹15,000 a month. She owns no house anywhere and receives no HRA. Her total income before section 134 is ₹6,00,000. Compute the deduction.

jobs.title: Regime comparison for an employee
jobs.situation: An employee asks whether deductions justify leaving the default regime.
steps: List eligible deductions under the optional regime.
jobs.takeaway: Only large deductions beat the default regime slabs.

mcqs.explain: Individuals and HUFs. In practice: not in default regime.

He pays: PPF ₹1,00,000; life insurance premium ₹80,000 (within the premium limits); own NPS ₹50,000 (not claimed elsewhere); health insurance for self and family ₹30,000; health insurance for his parents (both above 60) ₹55,000; and has savings bank interest of ₹14,000. summary: Deductions capped at GTI; not against special-rate income.
remember: Default regime keeps employer NPS and section 146.
traps: Allowing section 123 under the default regime.

viva.q: Can Chapter VIII deductions reduce LTCG on listed shares?
viva.model: They are barred against such special-rate gains; they come off the rest of gross total income only.

viva.q: What is the employer NPS limit for a private employee under the default regime?
How is the section 128 deduction computed?
viva.model: Actual expenditure on specified diseases up to ₹40,000, or ₹1,00,000 for senior citizens, reduced by insurance reimbursement.

viva.q: Who can claim rent deduction under section 134?
viva.model: Individuals with rent paid for their home who get no house rent allowance and own no residence at the place of work, filing the prescribed declaration.

viva.q: What turnover limit applies to an eligible start-up?
viva.model: Turnover up to ₹300 crore in the year of claim.

cases.title: Nimbus Robotics
cases.case: Nimbus Robotics Pvt Ltd, incorporated in 2022 with an IMB certificate and turnover of ₹40 crore, earns business profits of ₹6 crore in T.Y. 2026-27 from its eligible business. Its accounts are audited. During the year it hired new eligible employees with additional employee cost of ₹40,00,000.

mcqs.q: Maximum section 140 deduction if this is one of its chosen years (₹):
mcqs.explain: 100% of eligible profits. In practice: GTI cap.

mcqs.explain: 30% × 40,00,000. In practice: repeat for two more years.
